findings.title: Race condition causes lost match_count increments
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does a read-modify-write on match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) without any locking. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will each read the same match_count, both increment to N+1 in memory, and both persist N+1, losing one increment. Because this is invoked from the EmailValidator on the signup path, multiple simultaneous attempts to register with a blocked email will undercount the hits, breaking the audit/statistics this feature is built around. Use an atomic SQL update (e.g., BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)) or wrap in a row-level lock / SELECT FOR UPDATE.

findings.title: should_block? performs a DB write during read-only validation
findings.body: should_block? is named like a predicate but has the side effect of incrementing match_count and updating last_match_at whenever a record exists. The EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) calls it on every email validation, including runs that ultimately fail to save the user. Consequences: (1) match_count gets incremented even when the signup ultimately fails for unrelated reasons, distorting statistics; (2) every blocked-email signup now performs an extra UPDATE on the blocked_emails table inside what should be a validation pass, increasing contention; (3) if record.save fails it is silently swallowed, leaving an inconsistent mix of "returned true because record existed" but with no recorded hit. The hit-recording logic should be split from the block check (e.g., a separate should_record_hit?) and only run on successful user creation, or at least on a successful save of the record.

findings.title: Case-sensitive blocked-email lookup lets blocked addresses slip through
findings.body: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) with the raw, mixed-case value supplied by the user. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first is case-sensitive, and the migration's add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true is a plain btree unique index (not citext / functional lower(email) index). Existing flows normalize emails to lowercase in some places (e.g., users_controller#change_email uses Email.downcase), but neither the BlockedEmail model nor the validator does any normalization. An admin who adds 'Spammer@Evil.com' to the blocklist will not stop a signup from 'spammer@evil.com', 'SPAMMER@evil.com', etc. Worse, because the unique index is case-sensitive, you cannot even add both casings as separate rows. Normalize via before_validation (self.email = Email.downcase(self.email.to_s).strip) and either store lowercase + add a functional unique index, or use a citext column.

findings.title: Unique index on email does not enforce case-insensitive uniqueness
findings.body: add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true uses the raw column values, so 'spam@x.com' and 'SPAM@x.com' are treated as distinct and both can be inserted. Combined with the case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, this is the underlying cause of the bypass above and also makes it impossible for admins to comprehensively block an address. Use a case-insensitive column (citext) or a functional index such as add_index :blocked_emails, 'lower(email)', unique: true, name: 'index_blocked_emails_on_lower_email'.

findings.body: should_block? calls record.save with no error handling. If the save raises or returns false (e.g., a validation error on the BlockedEmail record, a DB error, or an ActionView::Template::Error from a future before_save), the exception bubbles up out of the EmailValidator and aborts user signup. The user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean validation message. At minimum, wrap in a rescue and log; ideally restructure so hit recording is not coupled to the block decision (see the related side-effect finding).

findings.title: rejectedEmails list never cleared and is case-sensitive
findings.body: rejectedEmails is initialized once as Em.A([]) and only ever pushObject'd to. It is never cleared, and the contains(email) check is case-sensitive. Consequences: (1) once a controller instance flags an email as rejected, the user cannot clear that rejection (e.g., if they fix a typo and try the corrected address it's fine, but if they re-type the same address with different casing, e.g. 'Bad@Spam.com' vs 'bad@spam.com', the rejection check silently misses it because the case-sensitive contains returns false even though the server already rejected it); (2) the array grows without bound for the lifetime of the controller. findings.title: Blocked-email check runs even when whitelist/blacklist already rejected the email
findings.body: The validator checks the whitelist/blacklist first and adds an error if appropriate, then separately calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value). The condition guards with `if record.errors[attribute].blank?`, which is correct in isolation. But should_block? also has the side effect of doing a DB write (updating match_count/last_match_at) for the matched record. Restructure so should_block? is a pure read with no side effects, and do hit-recording only on successful user save.

At least one spec should demonstrate that 'Foo@Spam.com' blocks 'FOO@spam.com' (after the model is fixed), and a spec using threads or raw SQL should illustrate the concurrent-update behavior so the regression is caught if someone removes the atomic update later.
